name: Kozmo.com
epitaph: Delivered in under an hour. Ran out of time.
oneLiner: A website that delivered videos, snacks, ice cream, magazines and more to your door in under an hour, with no delivery fee.
causeOfDeath: It delivered tiny orders for free across many cities, so every order lost money, and when investors stopped funding dot-coms it had no way to pay its riders.
moneyNote: About $250M is the total private funding reported by the Tufts Daily and Wikipedia; others say about $280M was spent. Its S-1 shows $113.6M raised in early 2000 alone. It closed and sold its assets; no buyer for the company.
inOneMinute: Kozmo promised to bring a DVD, a pint of ice cream or a magazine to your door **in under an hour, for free**. Think of it as 1999's Dunzo.
In 1999 it **lost about $7.54 for every $1 of revenue**. Average orders were tiny, around $10, and riders and warehouses cost a lot.
It expanded to 11 cities and promised Starbucks $150 million. When a last-minute merger fell through in April 2001, **all 1,100 staff lost their jobs**.
killerLine: **Free delivery is not free.** Someone pays for the rider, and if it isn't the customer, it is your runway.

chapters.title: The idea: anything, in under an hour
chapters.body: In March 1998, two young New York investment bankers, Joseph Park and Yong Kang, started Kozmo. The promise was magical: order **videos, games, music, books, snacks or basics** online and a rider on a bike would bring them to you in under an hour. **No delivery fee and no minimum order.** Students and young city workers loved it. A pint of ice cream, a magazine, a single DVD: Kozmo would bring it. If you have ever ordered from Dunzo, Blinkit or Zepto, you already understand the appeal. Kozmo was simply trying to do it in 1999, with no smartphones, no GPS apps and much more expensive technology. BusinessWeek even suggested it might become the 7-Eleven (corner shop) of the internet.

chapters.title: The rise: Amazon and Starbucks come calling
chapters.body: Investors rushed in. In late 1999, Kozmo raised $53 million in two rounds led by Flatiron Partners. **Amazon invested $60 million**, and the two agreed that Amazon customers could choose one-hour delivery for some books, music and toys. In February 2000, Kozmo signed a deal with Starbucks: it would **pay Starbucks $150 million over five years** for promotion in its cafés, and put drop boxes there for returning videos. That was roughly as much money as Kozmo had raised so far. In March 2000 it filed to list on the stock market. By July 2000 it was in **11 US cities**, from New York to Los Angeles, and planned many more.

chapters.title: The cracks: tiny orders, big costs
chapters.body: The S-1 (the document a company files before listing on the stock market) told the real story. In 1999 Kozmo made **$3.5 million in revenue and lost $26.4 million**. Delivery alone cost $3.3 million, nearly all its revenue. Marketing cost another $10.3 million. The problem was simple: when someone orders one small ice cream and pays nothing for delivery, the rider's time costs more than the profit on the order. In mid-2000 the average order was **only about $10**. Kozmo fought back. It added groceries, flowers and meals, started charging delivery on small orders, and pushed the average order up to $25. By December 2000, Boston, New York and San Francisco were profitable.

chapters.title: The fall: the money window slams shut
chapters.body: Kozmo's fixes came too late. By 2000 the dot-com crash had made investors terrified of loss-making internet companies, and Kozmo **never managed to list on the stock market**. In March 2001 it ended the Starbucks deal, having paid about $15 million. Its last hope was a merger with a Los Angeles grocery-delivery firm called PDQuick, which would have brought fresh money. That deal collapsed. On 11 April 2001 the website went dark and deliveries stopped in all nine remaining cities. Workers arrived to find the doors shut. **All 1,100 employees were let go.** The company said it had enough cash to pay staff and creditors, so it closed in an orderly way rather than going bankrupt.

charts.title: Revenue vs loss
charts.takeaway: As Kozmo grew, its losses grew much faster than its revenue.

charts.title: Average order size
charts.takeaway: Bigger baskets were the fix, and they worked, but only after most of the money was gone.

mistakes.title: Free delivery on tiny orders
mistakes.explain: Kozmo charged **no delivery fee and set no minimum order**, so a rider might cycle across town for one ice cream. With average orders around $10, the money from each order could not cover the rider, the warehouse and the technology. In 1999, **delivery costs alone nearly equalled all revenue**.

mistakes.title: Spread across 11 cities too quickly
mistakes.explain: By July 2000 it was in 11 cities, each with its own warehouses and riders, and it planned more. The first three cities only turned a profit in December 2000. Every extra city added **fixed costs before it had enough orders** to pay for them.

mistakes.title: A $150 million promise to Starbucks
mistakes.explain: Kozmo agreed to pay Starbucks **$150 million over five years**, about as much as it had raised at the time. Paying huge sums for promotion is a bet that the money will keep coming. When funding dried up, the deal became a weight around its neck.

mistakes.title: Fixed the basket too late
mistakes.explain: Raising the average order from $10 to $25 and charging for small orders did work. But Kozmo made these changes **only after investors had turned away** from dot-coms. If it had set a minimum order at the start, it would have needed far less outside money.

warningSigns: Does an average delivery cost you more than it brings in, counting the rider's time?
Can a customer order one cheap item and still get free delivery?
Are you opening a second city before the first one is profitable?
Have you signed a long marketing or partnership deal that you can only afford if you raise again?
Would your company die within months if your next round or merger fell through?

lessons.title: Set a minimum basket from day one
lessons.detail: Quick-commerce apps in India use minimum order values and small delivery fees for a reason. Work out the smallest order that covers the rider's trip, and do not deliver below it for free.

lessons.title: Grow basket size before city count
lessons.detail: Kozmo's best move was raising the average order from $10 to $25. Add products people buy together (snacks with drinks, groceries with household items) so each trip earns more.

lessons.title: Be careful with big fixed promises
lessons.detail: A deal to pay a partner a fixed amount every year is like a loan. Before signing, ask: can we still pay this if no investor gives us money for 18 months?

lessons.title: Have a plan that does not need a rescue
lessons.detail: Kozmo's survival depended on a merger. When it failed, the company died the same week. Always keep a 'smaller but alive' plan: fewer cities, fewer staff, profitable core.

lessons.title: Great ideas can be early
lessons.detail: People clearly wanted fast delivery. What was missing in 1999 was cheap smartphones, GPS routing and dense dark stores. If your idea is loved but the costs don't work yet, ask what would have to change, and when.

quote.text: The fit between Kozmo.com and Starbucks is a natural one.
quote.who: Joseph Park, co-founder and CEO of Kozmo.com
quote.context: Announcing the $150 million, five-year Starbucks deal in February 2000, about a year before Kozmo shut down

afterlife.text: Kozmo's former CTO, Chris Siragusa, started a smaller delivery service called MaxDelivery in Manhattan in 2005. The Kozmo brand was bought and relaunched more than once, without much success. Joseph Park later co-founded Askville, which became part of Amazon, and in 2009 became president of BibleGateway.com. A documentary, 'e-Dreams', captured Kozmo's story. Today the one-hour, then ten-minute, delivery idea is everywhere, including in India, run by companies with smartphones, GPS and delivery fees that Kozmo never had.

disputed.claim: When Kozmo started charging for delivery
disputed.note: One source says it charged on orders under $30; another says a $10 minimum came in early 2001. The exact rule and date are unclear.

disputed.claim: Number of cities at the end
disputed.note: It peaked at 11 cities in July 2000; at shutdown, reports say nine cities.
